plan.topic: Tirzepatide injection site reactions: redness, itching or a small lump. What's normal, what the label reports, and when to call
plan.angle: Answer within 10 s: mild redness, itching or a small bump where you injected was reported in the trials and is usually mild. Use the current Zepbound label's injection-site reaction rates exactly as printed: every dose arm vs placebo, with the label's own list of included terms (bruising, redness, itching, pain, rash). For the new fact, use a verified source: either the label's hypersensitivity figures (5% vs 3% on placebo; immediate reactions 2.1% vs 0.4%) or Taj et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2026, saying injection-site reactions were most often reported with tirzepatide among GLP-1 medicines and were dose-related. Drop the Cureus 156/5,066 figures unless the paper is opened and the numbers are found printed in it. Credit site rotation only to the Instructions for Use. Red flags: spreading redness, warmth or pus means calling your prescriber. Swelling of the face, lips or throat, or trouble breathing, means emergency care (label wording). Keep the Exp F line, 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line and 'don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own'.
plan.why: Proven calm body-worry 'is this normal?' format (median about 104) on a fresh fear we haven't covered, with a new meta-analysis fact. It also tests demand for the planned injection-site long-form. | fact-check: The topic is a good body-worry reassurance fit. The Zepbound label reports injection site reactions in about 6–8% of people (by dose) vs about 2% on placebo, and hypersensitivity reactions in about 5% vs 3%. I could not verify the 'new fact': a 2026 Cureus semaglutide meta-analysis with injection-site reactions at 156/5,066 vs 114/3,483 and very low certainty. The closest Cureus 2026 review I found doesn't match that description, and crediting it unverified is a hold risk. It's also semaglutide-only context in a tirzepatide Short. A better-sourced new fact comes from the label itself or Taj et al., DOM 2026: injection site reactions were dose-related and were reported most often with tirzepatide (about 2–7%) among GLP-1 medicines.

Redness, itching or bruising after your tirzepatide shot can be normal: injection site reactions are a listed side effect. Here's what the Zepbound label reports and when it's time to call your prescriber.

social.instagram_caption:
Itchy spot after your tirzepatide shot? It can be normal: it's a listed side effect.

Here's what the Zepbound label reports:
- In the label's weight-loss trials, injection site reactions (bruising, redness, itching, pain or rash) were reported in 6–8% of people on tirzepatide, depending on dose, vs about 2% on placebo.
- Allergic-type reactions, mostly skin ones like rash or itching, happened within a day of a dose in about 2% on tirzepatide vs under 0.5% on placebo. Severe reactions were rare, about 1 in 1,000.
- One easy habit from the official instructions: rotate your injection site every week.
- Spreading, warm redness or pus? Call your prescriber. Swelling of your face, lips or throat, or trouble breathing? Get emergency help right away.

Save this for your next shot day.

factcheck.summary: I checked every number against the Zepbound Prescribing Information (Revised 8/2026), and they all match. Table 1 for the weight-reduction trials gives injection site reactions of 6% on 5 mg, 8% on 10 mg and 8% on 15 mg, versus 2% on placebo. The footnote lists bruising, erythema, pruritus, pain and rash, which matches the script. Section 6.1 gives 2.1% vs 0.4% for allergic (hypersensitivity) reactions within one day of a dose, says most were skin reactions like rash or itching, and gives severe reactions as 0.1% vs 0%, so "about one in a thousand" is right. The weekly site-rotation advice is confirmed by PI Section 2.4 ("Rotate injection sites with each dose") and by the Medication Guide ("Change (rotate) your injection site with each weekly injection"). The Medication Guide also lists swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat and problems breathing as reasons to get medical help right away. The framing is accurate: rates are given against placebo, the population is the weight-loss trials, and nothing is overstated. The hook pays off its question. The tone is calm, the safety and prescriber lines are present, and the Short is about 150 words. I found no factual errors. There are 3 minor fixes, all about source tags and wording.

issues.claim: Spreading, warm redness or pus? Call your prescriber. (tagged src3, the Medication Guide)
issues.problem: The Medication Guide and the PI don't mention warm, spreading redness or pus (signs of infection). That half of the line is our own safety advice, but it carries the src3 tag. Our craft rules say our own safety lines get no source tag. The emergency half of the line (face, lip or throat swelling, trouble breathing) is in the Medication Guide.
issues.fix: Keep the narration as it is. Make sure no public field (description, sources) credits the infection signs to the Medication Guide. In the shot list, tag only the two emergency items to src3 and leave 'Spreading, warm redness or pus: call prescriber' untagged.

issues.claim: The instructions for use say to change your injection site each week. (src2, the IFU PDF)
issues.problem: I couldn't read the IFU PDF to confirm the exact wording. The same instruction is confirmed in PI Section 2.4 ('Rotate injection sites with each dose') and in the Medication Guide ('Change (rotate) your injection site with each weekly injection').
issues.fix: Change s4 source_ids to ["src1", "src3"]. Change the narration to: "One simple habit: the official patient instructions say to change your injection site each week." Alternatively, keep src2 only after someone confirms the IFU sentence by hand.

issues.claim: Tirzepatide 5–15 mg vs ~2% placebo, weight-loss trials
issues.problem: Muted-viewer test: the narration says 'depending on dose' but never says the dose range. It isn't misleading, but the card is more specific than what's spoken.
issues.fix: Change the stat_label to "Tirzepatide, all three doses, vs ~2% placebo, weight-loss trials", or add 'across the three doses studied' to the narration.

audio.soundNotes: Music sits right in the -12 to -15 dB window already; nudged it up slightly (x1.1) so it breathes more in pauses (~-14 dB) without crossing the ceiling under speech. Thinned several 3-4-deep simultaneous-cue stacks (the zoom reveal at ~7.9s, the chip bursts at ~21-22s, 38s, 46s, 50s, 54-60s, 64-73s) down to one or two sounds each by dropping redundant doubled swooshes/whooshes/ticks layered on the same swell or transition. Pulled down a handful of cues that measured too hot during speech (blips/pop around 8.7-9.2s and the swoosh at 65.9s) into the -14 to -20 dB felt zone, and left the already-quiet pause-timed swells (7.9s, 24.4s) alone since they're correctly louder in silence. Added a few bespoke texture hits (itch scratch, alert chime, resolve bell, calm pulse) to underline the emotional arc without adding extra stock-kit clutter.
